lesson.title: The Long Run Wait: Mean of a Geometric Distribution
lesson.summary: The expected number of trials until a first success has an unusually tidy formula, 1/p, that ties directly to how rare or common that success is.
lesson.body:
For a geometric random variable X with success probability p, the mean, the expected number of trials needed to get the first success, has a formula about as simple as formulas get: E(X) = 1 / p.

The intuition is easiest to see through the value of p itself. If a success happens with probability 1/2 on each trial, successes are common, and you'd expect to wait only 2 trials on average. If a success happens with probability 1/6, like rolling a specific number on a die, successes are rarer, and you'd expect a longer average wait of 6 trials. In general, a rarer success (a smaller p) means a larger 1/p, and a longer expected wait, which lines up with common sense before any formula gets involved.

Apply it to the die rolling example from earlier in this unit: rolling a fair six sided die until a 6 appears has p = 1/6, so E(X) = 1 / (1/6) = 6. On average, it takes 6 rolls to see a first 6, matching the intuitive sense that a die numbered 1 through 6 should take about 6 tries to land on any particular face. For the carnival game from the previous chapter, p = 0.2, so E(X) = 1 / 0.2 = 5. A player should expect, on average, to need 5 spins before winning a first prize.

It's worth seeing why this formula is at least plausible, even without a full derivation. Go back to the fair coin distribution built earlier, where P(X=1)=0.5, P(X=2)=0.25, P(X=3)=0.125, and P(X=4)=0.0625. The expected value is found the usual way, by multiplying each value of X by its probability and adding: 1(0.5) + 2(0.25) + 3(0.125) + 4(0.0625) = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.375 + 0.25 = 1.625 just from the first four terms. That partial sum is already climbing toward 1/p = 1/0.5 = 2, and every additional term from X=5, 6, 7 onward, each smaller than the last, keeps pushing the running total closer to exactly 2 without ever overshooting it.
